lessons.title: Case Study: How Costs Eat a High-Frequency Strategy on Bank Nifty

children.text: This case study uses only the explicit cost stack built across this chapter, brokerage, STT, exchange charges, SEBI fees, and GST. No slippage, no market impact, nothing from Chapter 3 is included yet. The point is to show how much damage the predictable, statutory side of trading costs alone can do to a strategy that trades often, before the harder-to-model costs are even added in.
The Strategy: Bank Nifty Futures Intraday Scalping

A quant analyst aspirant builds an intraday scalping strategy on Bank Nifty futures: short-horizon entries and exits based on order flow imbalance, averaging 8 round trips a day across roughly 250 trading days a year. Each round trip trades an average notional of ₹9,00,000 against ₹10,00,000 of deployed margin capital. Backtested purely on price, before any cost is applied, the strategy shows a gross edge of 0.035% of notional per round trip, the kind of thin, repeatable edge scalping strategies are built around.

Running the trade_cost function built in Lesson 3 on a ₹9,00,000 equity futures buy and sell, through a discount broker, gives an exact round-trip cost.

body.caption: Cost of one round trip, ₹9,00,000 notional, Bank Nifty futures, discount broker

body.text: Notice how lopsided this round trip is. The buy side costs ₹62.84, dominated by the flat ₹20 brokerage cap and stamp duty. The sell side costs ₹224.84, almost entirely because futures STT applies only there. A round-trip cost of ₹287.68 is not two equal halves, it is one cheap leg and one expensive leg, and STT alone accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total.

children.text: Why High Frequency Is So Exposed

The gross edge here was 0.035% of notional per round trip. The transaction cost was 0.032% of notional per round trip. Those two numbers being almost equal is not a coincidence built into this example, it is exactly the situation high-frequency strategies live in by construction. A strategy that trades 2,000 times a year is, almost by definition, chasing an edge measured in a handful of basis points per trade, because larger, less frequent edges get arbitraged away or simply do not exist that often. The transaction cost stack, meanwhile, does not care how thin the edge is, STT, brokerage, and the rest are charged at the same rate regardless. High turnover does not just add up costs, it forces the edge and the cost onto the same tiny scale, where a strategy can be profitable and nearly unprofitable at the same time, separated by a fraction of a basis point.

body.text: And this case study has not touched slippage or market impact at all, the subject of Chapter 3. A strategy already surviving on an 8.7% margin over its explicit transaction costs, 0.035% gross edge against 0.032% pure transaction cost, has essentially no room left to absorb bid-ask spread or market impact on top of this. Chapter 3 picks up exactly where this case study leaves off.

body.label: Breakeven Gross Edge, Transaction Costs Only
body.context: Below this, explicit transaction costs alone make the strategy unprofitable, before slippage or market impact are even added.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: This strategy trades 8 round trips a day. If it instead traded only 2 round trips a day, holding notional per trade and the per-trade cost the same, what happens to its total annual transaction cost?
options: It drops to about a quarter of the original
body.explanation: Total annual transaction cost is round trips per year multiplied by cost per round trip. Cutting round trips per day from 8 to 2 is a quarter of the original trade count, so total annual cost falls to roughly a quarter as well, from about ₹5,75,360 to about ₹1,43,840, freeing up far more of the gross edge to reach the bottom line.

body.text: A high-frequency strategy does not just pay transaction costs more often, it is forced to compete with them on the same tiny scale as its own edge. When gross edge per trade and transaction cost per trade sit within a hair of each other, as they did here, 91% of a year's gross profit can vanish into brokerage, STT, and GST before slippage ever enters the picture.

points: A Bank Nifty futures scalping strategy with a 63% gross CAGR fell to a 5.46% net CAGR once only explicit transaction costs, no slippage yet, were applied, because costs consumed 91.3% of gross profit.
The futures round trip was sharply asymmetric: the sell side cost roughly 3.6 times more than the buy side, driven almost entirely by STT applying only to the sell leg.

High-frequency strategies are structurally exposed to transaction costs because their per-trade edge and their per-trade cost tend to sit on the same small scale, unlike lower-turnover strategies where cost is a rounding error against the edge.
This entire result used only the Chapter 2 cost stack; slippage and market impact, covered starting in Chapter 3, would erode the already thin remaining margin further.
